systems.name: France
systems.intro: France invented the modern appellation system (AOC, 1935): each area has a specification (cahier des charges) that sets boundaries, grapes, yields and ageing, overseen by INAO.

levels.label: AOP / AOC
levels.txt: A delimited area with grapes, yields, alcohol and ageing set out in its specification. It guarantees origin and a style tied to the place.

levels.label: IGP
levels.txt: A broader area with more flexible rules (more grapes, higher yields). It guarantees origin while leaving freedom of style.

levels.label: Vin de France
levels.txt: Wine from anywhere in France, with no area on the label; it may state the grape and vintage.

label_example.extra_txt: The wine was bottled at the very estate that grew the grapes.

systems.sources: INAO (inao.gouv.fr); cahiers des charges of each AOC

systems.name: Italy
systems.intro: Italy arranges its wines in a pyramid: DOCG and DOC (which count as PDO for the EU) set the zone, grapes, yields and ageing; IGT/IGP allow more freedom, and plain 'Vino' states no origin.

levels.label: DOCG
levels.full: Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita
levels.txt: The top tier: strict rules and a tasting panel check before release. There are 79.

levels.label: DOC
levels.txt: A defined zone with its own rulebook (disciplinare) for grapes, yields and ageing. There are 332.

levels.label: IGT / IGP
levels.txt: Regional origin with more flexible rules; many famous reds were born here, outside the DOCs.

levels.label: Vino
levels.txt: Wine that meets neither PDO nor PGI requirements; origin is not guaranteed.

label_example.mention: Barolo Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita
label_example.extra_txt: In Barolo, Riserva requires at least 62 months of ageing (18 in wood) versus 38 for regular Barolo.

systems.sources: Italian Wine Central (Italian quality levels: 79 DOCG, 332 DOC, 111 IGP); Barolo DOCG profile

count.source: eAmbrosia (411 DOP) e Italian Wine Central (lista nov-2025)

systems.name: Greece
systems.intro: Greece follows the EU scheme: wines from historic zones are PDO (ΠΟΠ) and regional wines are PGI (ΠΓΕ); below them sit varietal wines without origin and table wine.

levels.label: PDO (ΠΟΠ)
levels.full: Protected Designation of Origin / Prostatevomeni Onomasia Proelefsis
levels.txt: Historic wine zones with regulated grapes and winemaking; it brings together the former OPAP and OPE.

levels.label: PGI (ΠΓΕ)
levels.full: Protected Geographical Indication / Prostatevomeni Geografiki Endeixi
levels.txt: Regional wines ('topikos oinos') with more permitted varieties, international ones included.

levels.label: Varietal
levels.txt: May state grape and vintage, but no geographical area.

levels.label: Wine
levels.txt: No origin, grape or vintage on the label.

label_example.mention: Santorini Protected Designation of Origin (ΠΟΠ Σαντορίνη)
label_example.extra_txt: Traditional Santorini term: dry white with at least 3 months in barrel and a minimum of 13.5% alcohol.

systems.name: Hungary
systems.intro: Hungary uses the EU system under its own names: OEM for designations of origin (PDO) and OFJ for regional wines (PGI); Tokaj also has its own rules for its sweet wines.

levels.label: OEM (PDO)
levels.txt: Quality wine from one of the 22 wine regions (borvidék) or smaller appellations, with its own rulebook.

levels.label: OFJ (PGI)
levels.txt: Regional wine (tájbor) from one of six large areas, with broader rules.

levels.label: Bor
levels.txt: Wine with no indication of origin.

label_example.mention: Tokaji Aszú — Oltalom alatt álló eredetmegjelölés
label_example.extra_txt: May only appear on an Aszú with at least 150 g/l of residual sugar.

systems.name: Spain
systems.intro: Each DO has a Regulatory Council (Consejo Regulador) that sets the area, grapes, yields and minimum ageing. On top of that, the ageing terms (Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva) tell you how long the wine spent in barrel and bottle.

levels.label: Vino de Pago
levels.txt: The single-estate category (created in 2003): grapes from the estate's own vineyards, made and bottled by its owners.

levels.label: DOCa / DOQ
levels.txt: A DO with at least 10 years of track record and stricter controls; sold only in bottle. Only Rioja and Priorat hold it.

levels.label: DO
levels.txt: A delimited area with a Regulatory Council that sets grapes, maximum yield and minimum ageing.

levels.label: Vino de la Tierra (IGP)
levels.txt: At least 85% of the grapes from the named area, with more flexible rules on grapes and winemaking.

levels.label: Vino
levels.txt: Wine without a protected origin: it can blend grapes from anywhere in Spain.

label_example.extra_txt: In Rioja, a red with 60 months of ageing, at least 24 of them in barrel.

systems.sources: Wine With Seth (Spain's DO hierarchy, Law 24/2003 and Law 6/2015); Basque Government (DOCa Rioja)

count.source: MAPA, Informe DOPs de vino 2024/2025 (106 DOP); IGP: eAmbrosia (UE) 2026

systems.name: Portugal
systems.intro: Each region has a certifying body (a Regional Wine Commission; in the Douro and for Port, the IVDP) that approves wines by analysis and tasting before granting the seal. Terms such as Reserva or Garrafeira add quality and ageing requirements.

levels.label: DOC / DOP
levels.txt: A delimited area with permitted grapes, maximum yield and minimum alcohol; every wine is examined by the regional commission.

levels.label: Vinho Regional (IGP)
levels.txt: Broad areas: at least 85% of the grapes from the region and more freedom to choose grapes, including international ones.

levels.label: Vinho
levels.txt: Basic wine without an appellation (formerly 'Vinho de Mesa').

label_example.extra_txt: Wine from a single outstanding vintage; for reds, at least 30 months of ageing, 12 of them in bottle.

systems.sources: Wine With Seth (Portuguese wine classification); IVDP (DOP Douro and Porto)

systems.name: Germany
systems.intro: There are 13 regions (Anbaugebiete). Traditionally wines are classified by grape ripeness (Prädikat), and since 2021 an origin pyramid has been added: the smaller the origin, the stricter the rules.

levels.label: Prädikatswein
levels.txt: Quality wine classified by grape ripeness (from Kabinett to Trockenbeerenauslese); no sugar may be added to the must.

levels.label: Qualitätswein
levels.txt: 100% from one of the 13 regions and with an official quality test.

levels.label: Landwein
levels.txt: Wine with a broad geographical indication (PGI), with more flexible rules.

levels.label: Deutscher Wein
levels.txt: Basic wine without a protected origin.

label_example.extra_txt: The first ripeness level of the Prädikat: light, fresh wines, often with some sweetness.

systems.sources: Wines of Germany (2021 origin pyramid); Wine With Seth (German classification)

systems.name: United States
systems.intro: The TTB's AVA (American Viticultural Area) system defines areas by their geography, soil and climate, but it does not regulate which grapes are planted, yields or ageing: it only guarantees where the grapes come from. Each state can add its own rules (Oregon is stricter).

levels.label: AVA
levels.txt: An area defined by its own features (climate, soil, terrain). Requires 85% of the grapes from the AVA and the wine to be finished in the AVA's state.

levels.label: County
levels.txt: Names a county (e.g. Sonoma County). Requires 75% of the grapes from that county.

levels.label: State
levels.txt: Names a state (e.g. California). Requires 75% of the grapes from the state, though some states require more.

levels.label: American Wine
levels.txt: Wine from US grapes with no more precise origin; it can blend states. Since 2012 it may carry a vintage, and it may also name a variety.

label_example.extra_txt: All the grapes come from vineyards owned or controlled by the winery within the AVA, and the wine was made and bottled there.

systems.sources: TTB 27 CFR 4.25/4.23 via winewithseth.com (label rules United States); Wikipedia (articles on each AVA, TTB/ATF dates)

count.source: TTB, 27 CFR parte 9 subparte C (eCFR, oct-2026)

systems.name: Australia
systems.intro: Geographical Indications (GIs) are set by the Geographical Indications Committee and registered by Wine Australia. They only mark geographical boundaries in a pyramid of zones, regions and subregions; they do not regulate grapes or yields. The '85% rule' applies to origin, variety and vintage, and is enforced by the Label Integrity Program.

levels.label: Subregion
levels.txt: Part of a region with even more uniform features (e.g. Pokolbin within Hunter).

levels.label: Region
levels.txt: Needs at least 5 independent vineyards of 5 ha or more, generally around 500 tonnes of grapes a year, and must be uniform and distinct from its neighbours.

levels.label: Zone
levels.txt: A broad geographical area within a state (e.g. Barossa, which includes Barossa Valley and Eden Valley).

levels.label: State / Super zone
levels.txt: A whole state or a super zone such as South Eastern Australia, designed for blends from several states.

levels.label: Wine of Australia
levels.full: Wine of Australia / Product of Australia
levels.txt: Mandatory statement of national origin; no more precise region.

label_example.extra_txt: Mandatory on every bottle sold in Australia.

systems.sources: winecompanion.com.au (Australian wine label laws); winewithseth.com (Australian geographical indications)

count.source: Wine Australia, Register of Protected GIs

systems.name: New Zealand
systems.intro: Wine GIs are registered with IPONZ under the Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits) Registration Act 2006, which came into force on 27 July 2017; regions have been registered since 2018. They only protect origin: there are no rules on grapes or yields.

levels.label: Subregional GI
levels.txt: A smaller GI within a region (e.g. Martinborough in Wairarapa). Same 85% rule.

levels.label: Regional GI
levels.txt: A registered region (Marlborough, Central Otago, Hawke's Bay...). At least 85% of the grapes from there and the rest from New Zealand.

levels.label: Island
levels.txt: Automatic, permanent GIs for each island.

levels.label: New Zealand
levels.txt: National GI, also automatic; grapes from anywhere in the country.

systems.sources: IPONZ (Marlborough GI register); sommjournal.com (New Act protects NZ GIs)

systems.name: China
systems.intro: China has no AOC-style pyramid of wine appellations. It protects some wines as 'geographical indication products' (地理标志产品), the same system it uses for other foods: Helan Mountain East Foothill (Ningxia) was recognised in 2003, among the first together with Changli, Shacheng and Yantai. Four of these wine GIs became protected in the EU under the 2021 EU–China agreement. Separately, Ningxia has a five-tier classification of wineries (not of areas).

levels.label: Geographical indication
levels.full: 地理标志产品 (Geographical Indication Product)
levels.txt: Protects the name of an area for its wine. There are few today: Helan Mountain East Foothill, Yantai, Shacheng and Huanren (ice wine) are the ones also recognised in the EU.

levels.label: Wine of China
levels.txt: Wine that only states a country or province, with no legal designation of origin.

label_example.mention: 贺兰山东麓葡萄酒 (Helan Mountain East Foothill)
label_example.extra_txt: A tier of Ningxia's winery classification (five tiers, from Fifth to First Growth); classified wineries may put it on the label.

systems.sources: grapewallofchina.com (EU–China GI agreement, 2021); winewithseth.com (Helan Mountain Eastern Foothills); decanterchina.com (Ningxia classification)

systems.name: Uruguay
systems.intro: Uruguay has no European-style appellations of origin: the law (Decree 283/993) classifies wines by quality as VCP or Vino Común, and lets the label name the department or area the grapes come from, with an INAVI certificate. The 'regions' INAVI uses (Metropolitana, Oceánica, Litoral, etc.) are groupings of departments for promotion and statistics, not legal categories.

levels.label: Geographical indication
levels.full: Geographical indication of origin (department or area)
levels.txt: Optional statement on a VCP: the place name (e.g. Canelones) can only be used if the grapes were grown there, and it requires an INAVI certificate. It has no rules of its own on grapes or yields.

levels.label: VCP
levels.txt: Wine from approved Vitis vinifera varieties, with at least 10.5% alcohol, lab testing, a glass bottle of up to 750 ml and a label registered with INAVI.

levels.label: Vino Común
levels.txt: Wine that doesn't meet the VCP requirements; usually sold in demijohns, cartons or bag-in-box and labelled 'Vino Común'.

label_example.extra_txt: Shows that the wine meets the quality requirements of Decree 283/993 and passed INAVI's inspection.

systems.sources: IMPO: Decree 283/993 (VCP, arts. 4, 8, 9, 11, 15–17) and Decree 431/994; INV Argentina, guide to Uruguayan regulations (2024); Wikipedia 'Uruguay wine'; winewithseth.com 'Uruguay wine law'.

systems.name: Argentina
systems.intro: Law 25.163 (1999) sets up three tiers of origin, overseen by the INV: Indicación de Procedencia, Indicación Geográfica and Denominación de Origen Controlada. There are over 100 GIs and only two DOCs: Luján de Cuyo and San Rafael.

levels.label: DOC
levels.txt: 100% of the grapes from the area, made and bottled there, from authorized varieties and with a maximum yield; overseen by a Promotion Council with its own rules and an approval tasting.

levels.label: IG
levels.txt: Quality wine made from 100% grapes from a defined area (province, department, valley or locality) and from varieties suited to quality wine.

levels.label: IP
levels.txt: Only for table or regional wines: at least 80% of the grapes grown and vinified in the named area.

label_example.mention: Denominación de Origen Controlada Luján de Cuyo
label_example.extra_txt: Ageing term that can only be used by wines from the varieties the INV authorizes for IG, DOC, Reserva and Gran Reserva.

systems.sources: Law 25.163 (arts. 3–5, 13–21) and Decree 57/2004 (argentina.gob.ar/normativa); INV Resolution C.32/2002; INV, Protection of Origin and list of GIs and DOCs (April 2024).

count.source: INV, listado de IG y DOC (18-abr-2024)

systems.name: Chile
systems.intro: Decree 464 (1994) divides the country into nested Denominaciones de Origen: regions, subregions (the 'valleys'), zones and areas (communes). It sets no grapes or yields: it guarantees origin. Since 2011, Costa, Entre Cordilleras or Andes can be added.

levels.label: DO
levels.txt: At least 75% of the wine from the named region, valley, zone or area (85% in practice for export); no limits on grapes or yields.

levels.label: Wine without DO
levels.full: Wine without an appellation of origin
levels.txt: Wine from wine grapes with no declared origin; it may state variety and vintage if they make up at least 75% of the total.

levels.label: Table-grape wine
levels.txt: Made from table grapes: it can't state variety, vintage or quality terms.

label_example.mention: Denominación de Origen Valle del Maipo
label_example.extra_txt: At least 1% alcohol above the legal minimum, with time in oak.

systems.sources: SAG: Decree 464 (1994), consolidated text (arts. 1, 3, 4, 5, 5 bis, 8–10) and Decree 27/2024 (Diario Oficial 14/05/2025); winewithseth.com 'Chilean wine classification'.

dos.name: Madiran
rules: Still red wines only.
Tannat: at least 60% of the vineyard and of the blend. Yield: 55 hl/ha.
Minimum natural alcohol: 11.5%.
Compulsory ageing in vessels over 100 L (not glass); release only from the year after the harvest (currently from 1 November; the draft amendment brings it forward to 1 May).
dos.soil: Clay-limestone over molasse on the west-facing slopes, and boulbènes (leached acidic silts) on plateaus and gentle hills.
dos.climate: Temperate and fairly humid, oceanic, with a warm, dry southerly wind (föhn-like) in late summer and autumn.
dos.txt: The home of Tannat: deeply coloured reds with powerful tannins that improve over years in bottle.
dos.sources: INAO, cahier des charges AOC Madiran (amendment draft, inao.gouv.fr)

dos.name: Chinon
rules: Reds and rosés from Cabernet Franc; Cabernet Sauvignon at most 10% of the vineyard.
Whites from Chenin Blanc only.
Yield: 55 hl/ha.
Minimum natural alcohol: 10.5% for reds and rosés, 10% for whites.
Reds may be released from 1 January following the harvest.
dos.soil: Gravels and sands of the Vienne valley, and slopes of tuffeau limestone and flinty clays from the Cretaceous.
dos.climate: Oceanic to semi-continental, warmer and drier than the rest of Touraine.
dos.txt: The benchmark for Loire Cabernet Franc: fresh reds with red fruit and herbal notes; lighter on gravel, more structured on limestone.
dos.sources: INAO, cahier des charges AOC Chinon 2026 (inao.gouv.fr)

dos.name: Saint-Émilion
rules: Red wines only.
Yield: 53 hl/ha.
Minimum natural alcohol: 11%.
Petit Verdot: at most 10% of the blend.
Ageing at least until 31 March following the harvest; release from 15 April. There is also the separate AOC Saint-Émilion Grand Cru (1954), stricter and with its own classification.
dos.soil: A limestone plateau above the Dordogne, with clay-limestone soils, silts and molasse slopes.
dos.climate: Bordeaux’s temperate oceanic climate, slightly more continental as it lies further east.
dos.txt: Merlot-led with Cabernet Franc: fleshy, velvety reds; those from the limestone plateau are the finest and longest-lived.
dos.sources: INAO, cahier des charges AOC Saint-Émilion (BO agri, arrêté 2023); INAO fact sheet Saint-Émilion Grand Cru

dos.name: Pauillac
rules: Red wines only.
Yield: 57 hl/ha.
Minimum natural alcohol: 11%.
Ageing at least until 1 June following the harvest; release from 1 September.
dos.soil: Deep, very free-draining gravel terraces, with sand and clay in the lower parts.
dos.climate: Temperate oceanic, moderated by the Atlantic and the Gironde estuary.
dos.txt: Home to three of the five Premiers Grands Crus of the 1855 classification (Mouton Rothschild was promoted to that rank in 1973): intense Cabernet Sauvignon with cassis, cedar and graphite, built to age for decades.
dos.sources: INAO, cahier des charges AOC Pauillac 2025 (inao.gouv.fr)

dos.name: Chablis
rules: White wines from Chardonnay only.
Yield: 60 hl/ha (Premier Cru: 58).
Minimum natural alcohol: 10% (Premier Cru: 10.5%).
Tiers: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Chablis Premier Cru and Chablis Grand Cru.
dos.soil: Always calcareous: marls with fossil oysters (Exogyra virgula, from the Kimmeridgian) and limestone beds.
dos.climate: Oceanic with continental influence; about 650 mm of rain and a high risk of spring frost.
dos.txt: Taut, mineral Chardonnay with lemon, green apple and a saline touch; almost no oak in the classic style.
dos.sources: INAO, cahier des charges AOC Chablis (PNO 2023, inao.gouv.fr)

dos.name: Meursault
rules: Whites from Chardonnay and Pinot Blanc; reds from Pinot Noir.
Yield: 57 hl/ha for whites, 50 hl/ha for reds (Premier Cru: 55 and 48).
Minimum natural alcohol: 11% for whites, 10.5% for reds.
Ageing at least until the following 15 March; release from 31 March.
dos.soil: Alternating Middle Jurassic limestones and marls, heavily fractured, with stony scree at the foot of the slope.
dos.climate: Cool oceanic, about 750 mm of rain, somewhat sheltered by the Morvan.
dos.txt: One of the capitals of Chardonnay: broad, unctuous whites with hazelnut, butter and ripe fruit that gain from barrel ageing.
dos.sources: INAO, cahier des charges AOC Meursault (PNO 2025, inao.gouv.fr)

dos.name: Bourgogne (Côte d'Or)
rules: Reds from Pinot Noir; whites from Chardonnay and Pinot Blanc.
AOC Bourgogne yield: 60 hl/ha for reds, 68 hl/ha for whites.
With the mention 'Côte d'Or' (grapes from the Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune only): 58 hl/ha for reds and 66 hl/ha for whites; minimum natural alcohol 10.5% for reds and 11% for whites.
Above it sit the village AOCs (Gevrey-Chambertin, Meursault...), the Premiers Crus and the Grands Crus.
dos.soil: Jurassic sediments, mainly limestones and marls.
dos.climate: Cool oceanic with regular rainfall and continental influence to the east.
dos.txt: The Côte d'Or is the strip of slopes that produces the world’s most famous Pinot Noirs; the mention 'Bourgogne Côte d'Or' identifies regional wine made only there.
dos.sources: INAO, cahier des charges AOC Bourgogne (PNO 2025, inao.gouv.fr)

dos.name: Languedoc
rules: Created in 1985 as Coteaux du Languedoc; called Languedoc since 2007.
Reds: main grapes at least 50% and Syrah + Mourvèdre at least 20% of the vineyard; Carignan and Cinsault at most 40% each.
Yield: 50 hl/ha for reds and rosés, 60 hl/ha for whites.
Minimum natural alcohol: 11.5%.
dos.soil: Highly varied, from schist to limestone and clay.
dos.climate: Mediterranean, between the mistral and the tramontane.
dos.txt: The great regional AOC of the south: fruity, spicy Mediterranean blends of Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre at good prices.
dos.sources: INAO, cahier des charges AOC Languedoc (PNO 2023, inao.gouv.fr); Hachette Vins

dos.name: Pomerol
rules: Red wines only.
Yield: 49 hl/ha.
Minimum natural alcohol: 11%.
Ageing at least until 1 November following the harvest; release from 15 November.
dos.soil: An almost flat plateau of gravel and sand over clay; blue clay in the centre.
dos.climate: Temperate oceanic, moderated by the confluence of the Isle and the Dordogne; warm summers and autumns.
dos.txt: A small area with no official classification, dominated by Merlot: silky reds with plum and truffle, among the most expensive in the world.
dos.sources: INAO, cahier des charges AOC Pomerol (PNO, inao.gouv.fr)

dos.name: Muscat du Ventoux
rules: It is a table-grape AOP, not a wine one.
Muscat of Hamburg only.
Maximum yield: 10 t/ha on trellis (13 t/ha on lyre).
Bunches of at least 250 g, hand-picked.
dos.soil: Sandy-silty-clay soils.
dos.climate: Mediterranean, very sunny and dry; Mont Ventoux cools the nights and breaks the mistral.
dos.txt: France’s only AOC for black table grapes: the Muscat of Hamburg from the foot of the Ventoux, bluish and highly aromatic.
dos.sources: INAO, cahier des charges AOP Muscat du Ventoux; INAO product sheet

dos.name: Sancerre
rules: Whites from Sauvignon Blanc only (AOC since 1936).
Reds and rosés from Pinot Noir only (since 1959).
dos.soil: Three soils: Kimmeridgian marls (terres blanches), limestones (caillottes) and flinty clays.
dos.climate: Cool semi-continental, with spring frosts; steep slopes from 180 to 350 m above the Loire.
dos.txt: The benchmark Sauvignon Blanc: citrus, herbal and mineral, with a gunflint touch on the flint soils.
dos.sources: INAO fact sheet and cahier des charges AOC Sancerre (inao.gouv.fr)

dos.name: Pessac-Léognan
rules: Yield: 54 hl/ha.
Minimum natural alcohol: 11%.
Whites: release from 30 March following the harvest; reds: from 1 October.
dos.soil: Gravels and pebbles, with patches of calcareous clay, sand and faluns.
dos.climate: Temperate oceanic, typical of the Gironde.
dos.txt: Northern Graves, home of Haut-Brion: Cabernet reds with smoky notes and some of Bordeaux’s finest dry whites.
dos.sources: INAO, cahier des charges AOC Pessac-Léognan (2026 draft, inao.gouv.fr)

dos.name: Côte-Rôtie
rules: Red wines only.
Syrah at least 80% of the blend; Viognier may be interplanted with the Syrah.
Yield: 40 hl/ha.
Minimum natural alcohol: 10.5%.
dos.soil: Very steep terraced slopes: pale gneiss on the Côte Blonde and dark mica-schist on the Côte Brune.
dos.climate: Semi-continental, with the cold north wind (the bise); southeast-facing slopes.
dos.txt: Northern Rhône Syrah with a little Viognier: perfumed reds of violet, black olive and pepper.
dos.sources: INAO, cahier des charges AOC Côte-Rôtie (PNO 2023, inao.gouv.fr)

dos.name: Cognac
rules: Double distillation in a copper Charentais still, completed by the following 31 March.
Minimum ageing of 2 years in oak.
Six crus delimited in 1938; Grande Champagne is the finest, and 'Fine Champagne' requires at least 50% Grande Champagne.
dos.soil: In Grande and Petite Champagne, shallow clay-limestone over soft Cretaceous limestone and chalk.
dos.climate: Temperate oceanic, about 13 °C on average with mild winters.
dos.txt: The most famous grape brandy: acidic, neutral Ugni Blanc, distilled twice and aged in oak. In the European Union it is registered as a geographical indication for a spirit drink, not as a wine appellation.
dos.sources: INAO, cahier des charges IG Cognac (PNO 2024, inao.gouv.fr)

dos.name: Armagnac
rules: Three areas: Bas-Armagnac, Armagnac-Ténarèze and Haut-Armagnac.
Distillation mainly in the continuous Armagnac still; double distillation is also allowed.
Minimum ageing of 1 year in oak. Blanche Armagnac (colourless, unoaked) has been a separate appellation since 2005 and rests at least 3 months in neutral vessels.
dos.soil: In Bas-Armagnac, reddish sables fauves (tawny sands) and acidic silts (boulbènes).
dos.climate: Oceanic in the west, with regular rainfall and no truly dry summer.
dos.txt: France’s oldest brandy; Bas-Armagnac gives the finest and fruitiest. In the European Union it is registered as a geographical indication for a spirit drink, not as a wine appellation.
dos.sources: INAO, cahier des charges IG Armagnac (PNO, inao.gouv.fr)

dos.name: Condrieu
rules: Whites from Viognier only.
Yield: 41 hl/ha.
Minimum natural alcohol: 11.5%.
With 45 g/L of sugar or more, from overripe grapes picked in several passes.
dos.soil: Poor sandy-clay soils of decomposed granite, with some loess.
dos.climate: Semi-continental Lyonnais mesoclimate, on steep south- and southeast-facing slopes; the bise, a dry north wind, dries the foliage.
dos.txt: The birthplace of Viognier: unctuous whites of peach, apricot and white flowers.
dos.sources: INAO, cahier des charges AOC Condrieu (PNO 2023, inao.gouv.fr)

dos.name: Champagne
rules: Second fermentation in bottle.
Pressing: at most 102 L of juice per 160 kg of grapes.
At least 15 months from tirage before release (36 months for vintage wines); disgorgement no earlier than 12 months.
dos.soil: A chalk subsoil that drains excess water and releases it in dry periods.
dos.climate: Dual influence: oceanic (regular rainfall) and continental (sometimes destructive frosts).
dos.txt: The sparkling wine par excellence: fine bubbles, high acidity and toasty notes from long ageing on the lees.
dos.sources: INAO, cahier des charges AOC Champagne (PNO 2026, inao.gouv.fr); champagne.education

dos.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
rules: Yield: 35 hl/ha.
Minimum natural alcohol: 12.5%.
A broad list of permitted varieties that can be blended freely.
dos.soil: Alpine rounded pebbles over red clay, plus sands and sandstones.
dos.climate: Mediterranean, with the mistral and about 2,800 hours of sunshine a year.
dos.txt: A pioneer of the AOC system (its 1923 rules, driven by Baron Le Roy, inspired the law) and one of the first AOCs of 1936: warm, spicy, powerful Grenache reds grown on the famous rounded pebbles.
dos.sources: Cahier des charges AOC Châteauneuf-du-Pape (chateauneuf.com, AOC growers’ syndicate)

dos.name: Sauternes
rules: Yield: 25 hl/ha.
Grapes with noble rot, hand-picked in successive passes, with at least 221 g/L of sugar.
Minimum natural alcohol: 15%; at least 45 g/L of residual sugar.
dos.soil: Varied: gravel, clay, sand and limestone.
dos.climate: Oceanic; morning mist from the Ciron river and afternoon sun favour Botrytis cinerea.
dos.txt: Sweet whites from nobly rotten grapes: honey, apricot and saffron, with acidity that makes them almost eternal.
dos.sources: INAO, cahier des charges AOC Sauternes (inao.gouv.fr)

dos.name: Alsace
rules: Yield: 80 hl/ha for whites, 60 hl/ha for reds.
Bottling compulsory in Alsace, in the 'Vin du Rhin' (flute) bottle.
A grape name on the label requires the wine to be made from that grape alone.

Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles mentions for sweet whites, only from Gewürztraminer, Pinot Gris, Riesling or Muscat; hand-harvested and released from 1 June of the second year after the harvest.
dos.soil: A mosaic: granite, schist, sandstone, limestone on the hills, and alluvium.
dos.climate: Semi-continental and dry (500–650 mm): the Vosges block rain from the west.
dos.txt: Aromatic single-variety whites, almost always labelled by grape: dry, mineral Riesling and exuberant Gewürztraminer. AOC since 1962 (the specification refers back to a 1945 ordinance).
dos.sources: INAO, cahier des charges AOC Alsace (PNO 2025, inao.gouv.fr)

dos.name: Bolgheri
rules: Rosso: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Cabernet Franc in any proportion; Syrah and Sangiovese up to 50% each
Superiore: at least 2 years of ageing, 1 in barrel, and 12.5% alcohol
Maximum yield: 9 t/ha for the Rosso and 8 t/ha for the Superiore
Created in 1984 as a DOC for whites; reds and rosés were added in 1994
dos.soil: A mix of gravel, clay, limestone and sand; mostly deep sandy clay loam with fine gravel.
dos.climate: Mediterranean, tempered by the sea breeze; wind on more than 250 days a year lowers humidity.
dos.txt: The Tuscan coast where the 'Super Tuscans' were born: Bordeaux blends of Cabernet and Merlot, powerful yet fresh. Sassicaia has had its own DOC since 2013.
dos.sources: Italian Wine Central (appellation profile); WineWiki winewithseth.com (soil and climate, citing the consorzio and disciplinare)

dos.name: Barolo
rules: 100% Nebbiolo
Minimum ageing 38 months, 18 in wood; Riserva 62 months
Minimum alcohol 13%
Maximum yield 8 t/ha
181 additional geographical mentions (MGA) to name vineyards and communes
dos.soil: Calcareous marls from the Tortonian and Messinian (Marne di Sant'Agata Fossili), with areas of sandstone and clay marls in Serralunga and Monforte.
dos.climate: Cool, temperate subcontinental, sheltered from the wind, between Alpine air and the humid air of the Tanaro valley.
dos.txt: The 'king of wines': pale-coloured reds that are highly tannic and acidic, with aromas of rose, tar and cherry, built to age for decades.
dos.sources: Italian Wine Central (appellation profile); WineWiki winewithseth.com (soil and climate, citing the consorzio and disciplinare)

dos.name: Brunello di Montalcino
rules: 100% Sangiovese (known locally as Brunello)
Released on 1 January of the fifth year after harvest, with at least 2 years in oak and 4 months in bottle
Riserva: one more year, with 6 months in bottle
Maximum yield 80 quintals/ha (8 t/ha); minimum alcohol 12.5%
dos.soil: Highly varied: sandstone, alberese and galestro, from sandy to clayey; poor, calcareous and low in water.
dos.climate: Dry Mediterranean with continental traits (about 700 mm of rain); Monte Amiata holds off storms and hail.
dos.txt: Pure, long-lived Sangiovese: intense reds with cherry, leather and herbs. DOC in 1966 and one of the first DOCGs (1980).
dos.sources: Consorzio del Vino Brunello di Montalcino (rules); Italian Wine Central (appellation profile); WineWiki winewithseth.com (soil and climate, citing the consorzio and disciplinare)

dos.name: Chianti Classico
rules: Minimum 80% Sangiovese; no white grapes since the 2006 vintage
Riserva: 24 months of ageing (3 in bottle); Gran Selezione: 30 months
Gran Selezione from the 2027 vintage: minimum 90% Sangiovese, the rest native grapes only
Maximum yield 7.5 t/ha; hillside vineyards up to 700 m
dos.soil: Galestro (clay schist), alberese (limestone) and calcareous sandstone; valley floors and heavy clays are excluded.
dos.climate: Continental, with cold winters, summers above 35 °C, wide diurnal range and 800–900 mm of rain.
dos.txt: The historic heart of Chianti, with the black rooster on the label: fresh Sangiovese with sour cherry, violet and firm tannins. Its own DOCG since 1996.
dos.sources: Italian Wine Central (appellation profile); WineWiki winewithseth.com (soil and climate, citing the consorzio and disciplinare)

dos.name: Prosecco
rules: Minimum 85% Glera
Spumante made only in pressurised tanks (Martinotti/Charmat method)
Rosé (since 2020): 85–90% Glera and 10–15% Pinot Noir, at least 60 days in tank and vintage-dated
Maximum yield 18 t/ha of Glera
dos.soil: Mostly alluvial, silty clay in texture with stones that aid drainage.
dos.climate: Temperate: the Alps block the cold from the north and the bora winds bring day–night temperature swings in late summer.
dos.txt: Italy's best-selling sparkling wine: light, fruity (pear, green apple, flowers) and made to drink young. The hillside versions are the Conegliano Valdobbiadene and Asolo DOCGs.
dos.sources: Italian Wine Central (appellation profile); WineWiki winewithseth.com (soil and climate, citing the consorzio and disciplinare)

dos.name: Amarone della Valpolicella
rules: Corvina and/or Corvinone 45–95%; Rondinella 5–30%
Grapes dried after the harvest (appassimento) until they reach at least 14% potential alcohol; they may not be pressed before 1 December
Minimum alcohol 14%
Minimum ageing 2 years; Riserva 4 years
dos.soil: White and pink marly limestones (Biancone, Scaglia Rossa), basalt outcrops and morainic and river deposits.
dos.climate: Continental to subcontinental, softened by Lake Garda; 850–1,000 mm of rain.
dos.txt: Dry red made from dried grapes: very concentrated and high in alcohol, with ripe black fruit, raisins and spice. Recognised as a style in 1968 and its own DOCG since 2010.
dos.sources: Italian Wine Central (appellation profile); WineWiki winewithseth.com (soil and climate, citing the consorzio and disciplinare)

dos.name: Orvieto
rules: Minimum 60% Grechetto and/or Trebbiano Toscano (Procanico)
Superiore: minimum alcohol 12%
Muffa Nobile: sweet wine from nobly rotten grapes, minimum alcohol 10.5%
Vendemmia Tardiva: harvest no earlier than 1 October
Classico: the historic zone, entirely in Umbria
dos.soil: Volcanic tuff, limestone and clay; marine fossils in some sectors.
dos.climate: Continental, moderated by altitude; autumn fogs from Lake Corbara encourage botrytis.
dos.txt: Fresh, citrusy whites around the city on its tuff crag, and a sweet botrytised rarity: Orvieto Muffa Nobile.
dos.sources: Italian Wine Central (appellation profile); WineWiki winewithseth.com (soil and climate, citing the consorzio and disciplinare)

dos.name: Vin Santo del Chianti
dos.area: Tuscany (Chianti area: Arezzo, Florence, Pisa, Pistoia, Prato, Siena)
rules: Minimum 70% Malvasia Bianca Lunga and/or Trebbiano Toscano; the Occhio di Pernice (rosé) has at least 50% Sangiovese
Grapes dried on mats or hung until they reach at least 260 g/l of sugar
Released on 1 November of the third year after harvest; Riserva, of the fourth
Minimum alcohol 13% (14% for Occhio di Pernice)
dos.txt: Tuscany's traditional dessert wine: dried grapes and long ageing in small casks (caratelli) of 15–50 litres; amber, with walnut, honey and dried apricot. Served with cantucci.
dos.sources: Italian Wine Central (appellation profile); Visit Tuscany (Vin Santo del Chianti DOC)

dos.name: Santorini
rules: Dry: minimum 85% Assyrtiko, the rest Athiri and Aidani
Sweet: minimum 51% Assyrtiko
Nykteri: at least 3 months in barrel and 13.5% alcohol
Vinsanto: at least 51% Assyrtiko, sun-dried grapes, at least 24 months in oak and 4 years before release
dos.soil: Volcanic: ash, pumice, basalt and sand, with almost no clay; ungrafted vines because phylloxera never arrived.
dos.climate: Very dry, windy Mediterranean (meltemi); moisture comes from the caldera fogs. Vines are trained into baskets (kouloura).
dos.txt: Razor-sharp, saline, mineral Assyrtiko whites that age well, and Vinsanto, a sweet wine from sun-dried grapes.
dos.sources: winesofgreece.org (PDO Santorini)

dos.name: Tyrnavos
rules: Muscat of Hamburg permitted in whites, rosés and reds
Dry, off-dry and medium-sweet whites and rosés; reds also sweet; semi-sparkling rosé
Rules revised in 2004 to add new varieties
dos.txt: Regional wine from the Thessalian plain, traditionally from Roditis and Muscat of Hamburg: aromatic rosés and reds, sometimes with a touch of sweetness.
dos.sources: winesofgreece.org (PGI Tyrnavos)

dos.name: Tokaj
dos.area: Northeastern Hungary (27 villages of the Zemplén)
rules: Aszú: minimum 120 g/l of residual sugar and 18 months in barrel
'6 puttonyos' only on Aszú with at least 150 g/l
Eszencia: free-run juice from aszú berries only, minimum 450 g/l of sugar
Dry Szamorodni: under 9 g/l of sugar; sweet: minimum 60 g/l and 6 months in barrel
dos.soil: Mostly volcanic and highly varied; loess on 5% of the area, near Tarcal and Tokaj.
dos.climate: Continental (10.8 °C average, 525 mm of rain); autumn river fogs bring noble rot and sunny afternoons shrivel the grapes.
dos.txt: Delimited in 1737 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site: birthplace of Tokaji Aszú, a sweet wine from botrytised grapes with very high acidity, and of dry Furmint.
dos.sources: WineWiki winewithseth.com (Tokaj PDO); wein.plus (Hungary)

dos.name: Rías Baixas
rules: Maximum yield 12,500 kg/ha (90 hl/ha).
'Rías Baixas Albariño' must be 100% Albariño, with at least 11.3% alcohol.
Five subzones: Val do Salnés, Condado do Tea, O Rosal, Soutomaior and Ribeira do Ulla.
'Barrica' wines are aged in wooden vessels of up to 600 litres.
dos.soil: Acidic, poor and shallow soils, in vineyards below 300 m.
dos.climate: Atlantic, with strong maritime influence and about 1,600 mm of rain a year; vines are trained on high pergolas because of the humidity.
dos.txt: The kingdom of Albariño: fresh, aromatic and saline whites, made beside the Atlantic rías.
dos.sources: AGACAL Xunta de Galicia (single document, DOP Rías Baixas 2024); Interempresas (history and rules of the DO)

dos.name: Vinho Verde
dos.area: Minho, northwest Portugal (9 subregions, including Monção e Melgaço)
rules: General maximum yield 10,666 kg/ha.
A wine may say 'Alvarinho' alone on the label only if it is 100% Alvarinho.
Must for Alvarinho needs at least 11% potential alcohol (8.5% in general).
The subregion term 'Alvarinho' is reserved for Monção e Melgaço.
dos.soil: Mostly granitic and acidic.
dos.climate: Atlantic and rainy; Monção e Melgaço is sheltered by mountains and has warmer, drier summers.
dos.txt: Light, fresh whites; Monção e Melgaço, the cradle of Alvarinho, produces the region's most intense and age-worthy whites.
dos.sources: Portaria 152/2015 (Informador.pt); Wikipedia and Wine With Seth (history and subregions); Forbes Portugal (Monção e Melgaço)

dos.name: Württemberg
rules: Qualitätswein: 100% grapes from the region and an official quality test.
'Schillerwein' is a protected rosé from Württemberg, made from red and white grapes fermented together.
Since 2021 the label follows the origin pyramid: growing area → Region → village → vineyard.
dos.soil: Very varied: shell limestone (Muschelkalk), Keuper, marls and loess.
dos.climate: Temperate; the Black Forest and the Swabian Jura shelter the valleys and the rivers moderate temperatures.
dos.txt: One of Germany's great red-wine regions (almost two thirds red grapes), famous for light Trollinger; Muskattrollinger (Muscat of Hamburg) is also grown there.
dos.sources: deutscheweine.de (Württemberg profile); Wine With Seth (Württemberg); vinoscout.de (Muskattrollinger)

dos.name: Rioja
dos.area: La Rioja, Álava and Navarra (Rioja Alta, Rioja Alavesa and Rioja Oriental)
rules: Standard yield 6,500 kg/ha for red grapes and 9,000 kg/ha for white.
Crianza: red with at least 1 year in barrel, released from its third year.
Reserva: red with 3 years of ageing, at least 1 in barrel.
Gran Reserva: red with 5 years of ageing, at least 2 in barrel.
dos.soil: Clay-limestone on terraces and benches, alongside sandy, silty and clay soils poor in organic matter.
dos.climate: Where Atlantic and Mediterranean climates meet, with mild temperatures and just over 400 mm of rain.
dos.txt: Spain's most famous DO: Tempranillo reds with barrel ageing as their hallmark. It was the country's first DOCa (1991).
dos.sources: riojawine.com (history and 2026 harvest rules); Basque Government (DOCa Rioja)

dos.name: Ribera del Duero
dos.area: Castilla y León, along the Duero (Burgos, Valladolid, Segovia, Soria)
rules: Reds with at least 75% Tempranillo; whites with at least 75% Albillo Mayor.
Maximum yield 7,000 kg/ha (9,500 kg/ha for Albillo Mayor).
Crianza: 24 months, 12 in barrel; Reserva: 36 months, 12 in barrel; Gran Reserva: 60 months, 24 in barrel.
Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva in oak barrels of up to 330 litres (the 'Roble/Barrica' mention allows up to 600).
dos.soil: Tertiary sands and clays and Duero river terraces, with basic pH and little organic matter.
dos.climate: Continental Mediterranean, dry, with extremes from 42 °C to −20 °C and 15–20 °C swings between day and night during ripening.
dos.txt: Powerful, deep Tempranillo reds, made on a high plateau with an extreme climate.
dos.sources: MAPA (DOP Ribera del Duero product specification, 2023)

dos.name: Priorat
dos.area: Tarragona, Catalonia (pre-coastal range, at the foot of Montsant)
rules: Maximum yield 6,000 kg/ha for red grapes and 8,000 kg/ha for white.
Reds with at least 13.5% alcohol.
Origin classification: DOQ Priorat → Vi de Vila → Vi de Paratge → Vinya Classificada → Gran Vinya Classificada.
Gran Vinya Classificada: max. 3,000 kg/ha, 80% of vines over 35 years old and at least 90% Grenache and/or Carignan.
dos.soil: Llicorella: very poor Palaeozoic slate, with bedrock 10–15 cm below the surface.
dos.climate: Dry Mediterranean: 400–500 mm of rain and a 14–15 °C average, with vines from about 200 to 700 m on steep slopes.
dos.txt: Concentrated, mineral reds from Grenache and Carignan on slate slopes; DOCa (DOQ) since 2000, the only one in Spain alongside Rioja.
dos.sources: Wine With Seth (Priorat DOQ, 2021 specification)

dos.name: Jerez-Xérès-Sherry
dos.area: Marco de Jerez, Cádiz (Jerez, El Puerto de Santa María, Sanlúcar de Barrameda)
rules: Minimum average ageing of 2 years (criaderas and solera system).
Fino: minimum 15% alcohol; Amontillado: 16%; Oloroso: 17%.
Maximum yield 11,428 kg/ha.
Fino Viejo: minimum average ageing of 7 years.
dos.soil: Albariza: soft white marl with 25–40% calcium carbonate, which holds moisture.
dos.climate: Warm, with more than 300 days of sun, about 600 mm of rain and Atlantic influence.
dos.txt: Fortified wines unique in the world: from dry Fino aged under a veil of flor to Oloroso and the ultra-sweet Pedro Ximénez.
dos.sources: Jerez Regulatory Council (product specification, May 2026)

dos.name: Cava
dos.area: Mainly Penedès (Comtats de Barcelona); also Valle del Ebro, Viñedos de Almendralejo and Requena
rules: Traditional method: second fermentation in the same bottle.
Minimum ageing on lees: 9 months; Reserva 18; Gran Reserva 30; Paraje Calificado 36.
Maximum yield 12,000 kg/ha (10,000 for Reserva and Gran Reserva; 8,000 for Paraje Calificado).
dos.soil: Mostly calcareous, somewhat clayey, poor in organic matter.
dos.climate: Mediterranean, transitional between coast and inland: about 2,500 hours of sun and 500 mm of rain.
dos.txt: Spain's great sparkling wine, made like Champagne; a DO defined by its method more than by a single territory.
dos.sources: MAPA (DOP Cava product specification)

dos.name: Port
dos.area: Douro valley (Baixo Corgo, Cima Corgo and Douro Superior)
rules: Alcohol between 19% and 22% (the dry 'leve' white may go down to 16.5%), fortified with 77% grape spirit.
Maximum yield 55 hl/ha for reds and 65 hl/ha for whites.
Colheita: a single vintage with at least 7 years in wood.
dos.soil: Stony schist (xisto) on very steep slopes, worked in terraces.
dos.climate: Continental: very cold winters and very hot, dry summers; the Marão and Montemuro ranges block the humid Atlantic winds.
dos.txt: The world's most famous fortified wine, sweet and powerful; its region, demarcated and regulated in 1756, is one of the first appellations of origin in history.
dos.sources: IVDP (DOP Porto technical dossier); Revista Jurídica / RCAAP (Companhia Geral, 1756)

dos.name: Douro
rules: Maximum yield 55 hl/ha for reds and rosés, 65 hl/ha for whites.
Reds with at least 11% alcohol (12% for those of very good quality).
Moscatel do Douro: fortified wine from Moscatel Galego Branco, between 16.5% and 22%.
Sparkling Reserva: at least 12 months in bottle after the second fermentation.
dos.soil: Schist predominates, with patches of granite.
dos.climate: Continental and dry, with average temperatures of 11.8 to 16.5 °C: 'nine months of winter and three of hell'.
dos.txt: The same vineyards as Port, but for dry wines: structured reds from local grapes and fresh high-altitude whites.
dos.sources: IVDP (DOP Douro technical dossier; Douro profile)

dos.name: Mosel
dos.area: Valleys of the Moselle, Saar and Ruwer (Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland)
rules: Since 2021 the label follows the origin pyramid: growing area (Anbaugebiet) → Region → village (Ort) → vineyard (Lage).
Village or vineyard wines: minimum ripeness at Kabinett level.
Großes Gewächs (dry wine from a Grosse Lage, a term that originated in the VDP association): hand-harvested, max. 50 hl/ha and a tasting examination.
dos.soil: Devonian slate in the Middle Mosel, clay slate and greywacke lower down and shell limestone in the Upper Mosel.
dos.climate: Cool but sheltered: the slate slopes store the day's heat; about half the vineyard has slopes steeper than 30°.
dos.txt: The mecca of Riesling (over 60% of the vineyard): light, very crisp and aromatic whites, from dry to sweet.
dos.sources: deutscheweine.de (Mosel profile); Wines of Germany (new 2021 origin pyramid); deutscheweine.de (region profile)

dos.name: Rheingau
dos.area: Hesse, north bank of the Rhine (Rüdesheim–Wiesbaden)
rules: Since 2021 the label follows the origin pyramid: growing area (Anbaugebiet) → Region → village (Ort) → vineyard (Lage).
Village or vineyard wines: minimum ripeness at Kabinett level.

Großes Gewächs (dry wine from a Grosse Lage, a term that originated in the VDP association; the Rheingau also has the historic 'Erstes Gewächs'): hand-harvested, max. 50 hl/ha and at least 12% alcohol.
dos.soil: Very varied in a small space: slate, quartzite, loess, sands, gravels and clays.
dos.climate: Mild winters and warm summers; the Taunus forests block cold winds and the Rhine reflects heat onto the vines.
dos.txt: A small, classic Riesling region (over 75% of the vineyard), with warmer, firmer wines than the Mosel; Assmannshausen is famous for its Pinot Noir.
dos.sources: deutscheweine.de (Rheingau profile); Wines of Germany (new 2021 origin pyramid); deutscheweine.de (region profile)

dos.name: Napa Valley
rules: If the label names the AVA, at least 85% of the grapes must come from there
If it names a grape, at least 75% of that variety
If it shows a vintage, at least 95% from that year
Contains 17 sub-AVAs (Rutherford, Oakville, Stags Leap District...)
dos.soil: San Pablo Bay sediments in the south and volcanic soils (lava and ash) in the north.
dos.climate: Mediterranean, with dry, hot summers; fog and Pacific air cool the afternoons and nights.
dos.txt: California's first AVA and the most famous name in American wine, above all for its powerful, ripe Cabernet Sauvignon.
dos.sources: Wikipedia (Napa Valley AVA); winewithseth.com (TTB rules)

dos.name: Russian River Valley
rules: If the label names the AVA, at least 85% of the grapes must come from there
If it names a grape, at least 75% of that variety
If it shows a vintage, at least 95% from that year
dos.soil: Sandy loams; Goldridge soil is famous for Chardonnay.
dos.climate: Cool: morning Pacific fog and nights about 20 °C cooler than the day.
dos.txt: A cool Sonoma valley dominated by Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, with juicy wines and good acidity.
dos.sources: Wikipedia (Russian River Valley AVA)

dos.name: Sonoma Coast
rules: If the label names the AVA, at least 85% of the grapes must come from there
If it names a grape, at least 75% of that variety
If it shows a vintage, at least 95% from that year
Includes the sub-AVAs Fort Ross-Seaview (2011) and West Sonoma Coast (2022), and overlaps with Russian River Valley and Petaluma Gap
dos.climate: Cool and rainy compared with the rest of Sonoma, due to the nearby Pacific.
dos.txt: A cold coastal AVA, a benchmark for taut, cool-climate Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
dos.sources: Wikipedia (Sonoma Coast AVA)

dos.name: Willamette Valley
rules: Under Oregon law, at least 95% of the grapes from the named AVA
Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and most grapes: at least 90% of the named variety
To use 'Oregon' on the label, 100% of the grapes must be from Oregon
dos.soil: Volcanic soils, marine sediments and loess.
dos.climate: Maritime and cool: rainy winters, dry and mild summers; almost no irrigation.
dos.txt: Oregon's first AVA and the home of the most Burgundian-style American Pinot Noir.
dos.sources: Wikipedia (Willamette Valley AVA); winewithseth.com (OAR 845-010-0905)

dos.name: Columbia Valley
rules: If the label names the AVA, at least 85% of the grapes must come from there
If it names a grape, at least 75% of that variety
If it shows a vintage, at least 95% from that year
Covers about 99% of Washington's vineyards
dos.soil: Loess sands and silts over gravel and basalt, left by the Missoula Floods.
dos.climate: Desert, due to the rain shadow of the Cascade Range; irrigated with river water.
dos.txt: Washington's great AVA: concentrated yet fresh reds thanks to intense sun and cold nights.
dos.sources: Wikipedia (Columbia Valley AVA)

dos.name: Walla Walla Valley
rules: If the label names the AVA, at least 85% of the grapes must come from there
If it names a grape, at least 75% of that variety
If it shows a vintage, at least 95% from that year
dos.soil: Mostly loess (wind-blown silt), very free-draining.
dos.climate: Hot days and cool nights, 250–500 mm of rain a year: irrigation needed; winters can reach -29 °C.
dos.txt: An AVA shared by two states, known for Cabernet, Merlot and above all very fruity Syrah.
dos.sources: Wikipedia (Walla Walla Valley AVA)

dos.name: Paso Robles
rules: If the label names the AVA, at least 85% of the grapes must come from there
If it names a grape, at least 75% of that variety
If it shows a vintage, at least 95% from that year
Since 2014 it has 11 sub-AVAs (Adelaida District, Templeton Gap District...)
dos.soil: Weathered granite and volcanic rock, with sandstone, shale and calcareous slates.
dos.climate: Warm and dry (250–635 mm of rain), with more than 40 varieties planted.
dos.txt: A warm, diverse area, strong in Cabernet, Zinfandel and Rhône grapes such as Syrah and Viognier.
dos.sources: Wikipedia (Paso Robles AVA)

dos.name: Monticello
rules: If the label names the AVA, at least 85% of the grapes must come from there
If it names a grape, at least 75% of that variety
If it shows a vintage, at least 95% from that year
dos.soil: Clay loams over a granite base.
dos.climate: Humid, 1,000–1,120 mm of rain; cold air drains down to the valley floors, leaving the slopes 2–3 °C warmer and with fewer frosts.
dos.txt: Named after Thomas Jefferson's home; Viognier and Cabernet Franc are its best-known grapes.
dos.sources: Wikipedia (Monticello AVA)

dos.name: Coonawarra
rules: If the label names the region, at least 85% of the grapes must come from there
If it names a grape, at least 85% of that variety
If it shows a vintage, at least 85% from that year
dos.soil: Red terra rossa over a limestone strip of about 15 × 2 km.
dos.climate: Maritime and cool (January ~19 °C), similar to Bordeaux.
dos.txt: Australia's most famous terra rossa strip: Cabernet Sauvignon with notes of mint and cassis.
dos.sources: Wikipedia (Coonawarra wine region); winecompanion.com.au

dos.name: Margaret River
rules: If the label names the region, at least 85% of the grapes must come from there
If it names a grape, at least 85% of that variety
If it shows a vintage, at least 85% from that year
dos.soil: Gravelly loams over granite and gneiss, with ironstone gravels.
dos.climate: Maritime, between the Indian and Southern Oceans; small temperature range and rain concentrated in winter.
dos.txt: A coastal region of elegant Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay, with a profile close to Bordeaux.
dos.sources: winewithseth.com (Margaret River); Wikipedia (Margaret River wine region)

dos.name: Barossa Valley
rules: If the label names the region, at least 85% of the grapes must come from there
If it names a grape, at least 85% of that variety
If it shows a vintage, at least 85% from that year
dos.soil: From clay loams to sandy loams.
dos.climate: Warm and dry, Mediterranean type.
dos.txt: The cradle of Australian Shiraz, with vines 100 to 150 years old: ripe, intense, spicy reds.
dos.sources: Wikipedia (Barossa Valley wine region)

dos.name: Eden Valley
rules: If the label names the region, at least 85% of the grapes must come from there
If it names a grape, at least 85% of that variety
If it shows a vintage, at least 85% from that year
dos.climate: Higher and cooler than Barossa Valley (climate region I).
dos.txt: Barossa's high-altitude neighbour, famous for dry, razor-sharp Riesling and fresher Shiraz. Its most planted grape is Shiraz (about 31%), followed by Riesling (24%).
dos.sources: Wikipedia (Eden Valley wine region)

dos.name: Hunter (Hunter Valley)
rules: If the label names the region, at least 85% of the grapes must come from there
If it names a grape, at least 85% of that variety
If it shows a vintage, at least 85% from that year
Subregions: Broke Fordwich (1997), Pokolbin and Upper Hunter Valley (2010)
dos.soil: Sandy alluvium (Semillon), deep loams (Shiraz) and patches of red volcanic soil, especially on the hills in the south of the valley.
dos.climate: Humid subtropical, one of the hottest and rainiest in Australia; rain at harvest is the big risk.
dos.txt: One of Australia's oldest regions; its unoaked, light and long-lived Semillon is unique.
dos.sources: Wikipedia (Hunter Valley wine region)

dos.name: Marlborough
rules: At least 85% of the grapes harvested in the named region
The rest must also be New Zealand grapes
dos.soil: Very free-draining alluvial gravels in the Wairau Valley; glacial loess in the Southern Valleys.
dos.climate: Sunny and dry, with cool nights from the sea breeze.
dos.txt: About 70% of New Zealand's vineyards; its aromatic, vibrant Sauvignon Blanc is a world style.
dos.sources: IPONZ (Marlborough GI register, 26/02/2018); Wikipedia (Marlborough wine region)

dos.name: Central Otago
rules: At least 85% of the grapes harvested in the named region
The rest must also be New Zealand grapes
dos.soil: Mica-rich silts over schist; very free-draining, irrigated.
dos.climate: New Zealand's only continental climate: semi-arid (375–600 mm), with a wide temperature range; vines at ~300 m.
dos.txt: The country's southernmost wine region: over 80% is Pinot Noir, with intense, pure fruit.
dos.sources: Wikipedia (Central Otago wine region)

dos.name: Hawke's Bay
rules: At least 85% of the grapes harvested in the named region
The rest must also be New Zealand grapes
Gimblett Gravels is not a GI: it is a trademark of its growers' association (~800 ha) within Hawke's Bay
dos.soil: Alluvial gravels (Omahu Gravels in Gimblett Gravels) and loams over pumice.
dos.climate: Warm and sunny, with cool coastal breezes at night.
dos.txt: New Zealand's red-wine region: Merlot and Syrah blends, especially from Gimblett Gravels.
dos.sources: Wikipedia (Hawke's Bay wine region; Gimblett Gravels)

dos.name: Helan Mountain East Foothill (贺兰山东麓)
rules: These rules belong to Ningxia's winery classification (2013), not to the GI.
Wineries can be classified into 5 tiers (Fifth to First Growth)
The classification is reviewed every 2 years; First Growth every 10
To be classified, a winery must grow its own grapes and make and bottle the wine on the estate
dos.soil: Alluvial gravel fans, wind-blown sands and grey steppe soils.
dos.climate: Semi-arid continental, under 200 mm of rain, ~3,100 hours of sunshine, vines above 1,000 m; winters of -20 °C mean the vines must be buried.
dos.txt: One of China's first wine GIs (2003) and its most awarded region: highly concentrated Cabernet and Marselan reds.
dos.sources: winewithseth.com (Ningxia Helan Mountain Eastern Foothills); decanterchina.com (Ningxia classification); grapewallofchina.com (EU–China agreement)

dos.name: Shacheng (沙城) – Huailai
dos.soil: Sandy loams and alluvial gravels from the Sanggan and Yang rivers, very free-draining.
dos.climate: Continental, ~370 mm of rain concentrated in summer and a wide temperature range; vines are buried in winter.
dos.txt: On Beijing's doorstep and home to Great Wall; Shacheng is the seat of Huailai, and the GI has been protected in the EU since 2021. Marselan is its flagship grape.
dos.sources: grapewallofchina.com (EU–China agreement); winewithseth.com (Hebei Huailai); thechinavine (Hebei terroir); Wikipedia (Huailai County)

dos.name: Canelones
rules: To put 'Canelones' on the label, the grapes must have been grown in the department (Decree 283/993, art. 17) and an INAVI certificate is required.
If the label names a variety, at least 85% of the wine must come from that grape.
As a VCP: at least 10.5% alcohol and a glass bottle of up to 750 ml.
dos.soil: Deep clays and silts that hold water.
dos.climate: Temperate and humid (1,000–1,200 mm), moderated by the Atlantic and the Río de la Plata.
dos.txt: It is the heart of Uruguayan wine: about two thirds of the country's vineyards (3,929 of 5,905 ha in 2023). It gives classic Tannat, full-bodied with rounded tannins, and plenty of Muscat of Hamburg.
dos.sources: INAVI, Vineyard Statistics 2023; IMPO Decree 283/993.

dos.name: Maldonado
rules: To put 'Maldonado' (or 'Garzón') on the label, the grapes must have been grown there (Decree 283/993, art. 17) and an INAVI certificate is required.
If the label names a variety, at least 85% of the wine must come from that grape.
As a VCP: at least 10.5% alcohol and a glass bottle of up to 750 ml.
dos.soil: Balasto: granite and ancient weathered rock, very well drained.
dos.climate: Temperate maritime, with a constant Atlantic breeze (Garzón is about 15–18 km from the sea).
dos.txt: Uruguay's new Atlantic zone (413 ha in 2023): fresher, saline wines, with benchmark Albariño and Tannat, especially in Garzón.
dos.sources: INAVI, Vineyard Statistics 2023; IMPO Decree 283/993.

dos.name: Luján de Cuyo
dos.area: Mendoza (Primera Zona, south of the city)
rules: At least 85% Malbec; the rest, other varieties authorized by the rules.
Maximum yield 10,000 kg/ha; vines 10 years or older and at least 5,000 plants/ha.
18 months between harvest and sale, with at least 6 months in oak.
Grapes with at least 13.5% potential alcohol; made and bottled at origin, with approval from a tasting panel.
dos.soil: Alluvial, from the Mendoza River: sand, silt and clay with stones, low in organic matter.
dos.climate: High-altitude desert (about 800–1,100 m), dry and sunny, with a wide diurnal range; irrigated with snowmelt.
dos.txt: Argentina's first DOC, created by growers in 1989 and recognized by the INV in 2005. Mid-altitude Malbec, fleshy with friendly tannins.
dos.sources: INV, Protection of Origin (Res. C 15/05); Los Andes (interview with R. de la Mota, 2021); iProfesional, 'Vinos con denominación de origen'; Cellar Tours, Luján de Cuyo.

dos.name: San Rafael
rules: 100% of the grapes from the area, made and bottled in San Rafael (Law 25.163, DOC).
Only authorized varieties, with a maximum yield set by the Promotion Council (Decree 57/2004).
dos.soil: Sandy alluvium with calcareous material and a stony subsoil.
dos.climate: Semi-arid (500–700 m), averaging about 15 °C, with a wide diurnal range and a risk of hail.
dos.txt: Argentina's second DOC (2007): an oasis in southern Mendoza, lower than the Primera Zona, with fruity Malbec and Bonarda and some whites.
dos.sources: INV, Protection of Origin (Res. C 31/07); Law 25.163 and Decree 57/2004; winewithseth.com 'San Rafael DOC'.

dos.name: Uco Valley
dos.area: Mendoza: departments of Tupungato, Tunuyán and San Carlos
rules: 100% of the grapes from the Uco Valley, from varieties suited to quality wine (INV Res. C.37/2002).
Within it are smaller GIs: Paraje Altamira, Los Chacayes, San Pablo, Pampa El Cepillo, Vista Flores, La Consulta and others.
dos.soil: Stony, sandy alluvium rich in calcium carbonate; in Gualtallary there are blocks with a lot of limestone.
dos.climate: High-altitude semi-arid (900 to over 1,700 m), under 250 mm of rain and a diurnal range of up to 20 °C.
dos.txt: Mendoza's high valley: fresh Malbec and Cabernet Franc with lively acidity and fine tannins; Gualtallary is its star district.
dos.sources: INV, list of GIs and DOCs (April 2024, Res. C.37/2002); winewithseth.com 'Uco Valley' and 'Gualtallary'.

dos.name: Cafayate Valley
rules: 100% of the grapes from the Cafayate Valley (synonym 'Cafayate'), from varieties suited to quality wine.
It lies within the larger GI Valles Calchaquíes / Valle Calchaquí (INV Res. C.37/2002; synonym added in 2010).
dos.soil: Sandy loam over alluvial gravel, very poor and free-draining.
dos.climate: High-altitude desert (1,650–2,000 m): under 250 mm, intense sun and a 15–20 °C diurnal range.
dos.txt: One of the highest vineyards in the world: very aromatic Torrontés and reds (Malbec, Tannat) with intense colour and tannin.
dos.sources: INV, list of GIs and DOCs (April 2024: Res. C.32/2002, C.15/04 and C.16/2010); winewithseth.com 'Cafayate'.

dos.name: Maipo Valley
dos.area: Subregion of the Central Valley (Santiago Metropolitan Region)
rules: At least 75% of the wine from the Maipo Valley (or its areas: Pirque, Puente Alto, Buin, etc.).
Variety and vintage on the label: at least 75% of what is stated.
'Andes' (e.g. Maipo Alto) requires 85% of the grapes from declared Andean areas.
dos.soil: In Maipo Alto, alluvial gravels and stones from the Maipo River; further toward the centre, deep clay loam.
dos.climate: Mediterranean, 300–400 mm of winter rain, with cold air flowing down from the Andes at night.
dos.txt: The cradle of Chilean Cabernet Sauvignon (over 60% of the vineyard). In Maipo Alto (Puente Alto, Pirque) it gives reds with black fruit, cedar and great ageing potential.
dos.sources: SAG, Decree 464 (subregion and areas, arts. 3–5 bis); winewithseth.com 'Maipo Valley' and 'Maipo Alto'.

dos.name: Casablanca Valley
dos.area: Subregion of the Aconcagua Region (Casablanca commune)
rules: At least 75% of the wine from the Casablanca Valley.
Variety and vintage on the label: at least 75% of what is stated.
It can add the term 'Costa' (85% of the grapes from coastal areas), with a special rule for Casablanca.
dos.soil: Clay, over decomposed granite.
dos.climate: Cool and coastal: morning fog from the Pacific and afternoon breezes.
dos.txt: Chile's first cool valley, planted from the 1980s: about 4,000 ha, three quarters white. Fresh, saline Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay.
dos.sources: SAG, Decree 464 (subregion, arts. 3–5 bis); wein.plus, 'Casablanca (Chile)'.

dos.name: Colchagua Valley
dos.area: Zone of the Rapel Valley (O'Higgins Region)
rules: At least 75% of the wine from the Colchagua Valley (areas such as Santa Cruz, Lolol, Marchigüe, Chimbarongo).
Variety and vintage on the label: at least 75% of what is stated.
Since 2018 it has its own micro-DOs, such as Apalta and Los Lingues.
dos.soil: Decomposed granite on the Apalta slopes; alluvial gravels and clay loam on the valley floor.
dos.climate: Warm, dry Mediterranean (400–600 mm in winter), cooled by the Pacific along the Tinguiririca River.
dos.txt: About 30,000 ha and Chile's great valley for ripe reds: full-bodied Carmenere and Cabernet Sauvignon, with Apalta as its iconic site.
dos.sources: SAG, Decree 464 (zone and areas); winewithseth.com 'Colchagua Valley' and 'Chilean wine classification'.

dos.name: Paraje Altamira
rules: 100% of the grapes from the delimited zone, from varieties suited to quality wine (Law 25.163). Recognized by INV Res. C.44/2013.
Lies within the Uco Valley GI; the original area was expanded in 2017.
dos.soil: Upper part of the Tunuyán River alluvial fan: large granitic stones coated in calcium carbonate, with sand and silt, highly variable within a few meters.
dos.climate: High-altitude desert, around 1,000–1,150 m, with a marked diurnal range and irrigation through canals from the Tunuyán River.
dos.txt: Perfumed Malbec (violet, red fruit), with mineral notes and a taut, elegant texture; also Cabernet Franc.
dos.sources: INV, listado de IG y DOC de la República Argentina (18/04/2024); Res. INV C.44/2013; Wines of Argentina, From terroir to GIs in Mendoza; Zuccardi, Guía del terroir del Valle de Uco; Decanter, Malbec Mendoza sub-zones

dos.name: Los Chacayes
rules: 100% of the grapes from the delimited zone, from varieties suited to quality wine (Law 25.163). Recognized by RESOL-2017-249-APN-INV#MA.
Lies within the Uco Valley GI; the INV extended its boundaries after recognition.
dos.soil: Heterogeneous sandy-loam and stony soils, with rounded stones coated in calcium carbonate, caliche and good drainage.
dos.climate: Arid to desert continental, with scarce rainfall; vineyards between about 1,000 and 1,350 m, among the warmest sectors of the Uco Valley.
dos.txt: Deeply colored, fruity Malbec with good acidity and firm, long tannins.
dos.sources: INV, listado de IG y DOC de la República Argentina (18/04/2024) (RESOL-2017-249-APN-INV#MA); El Cuco Digital, IG Los Chacayes y ampliación; La Nación, Tres regiones ganan fuerza; Zuccardi, ficha Aluvional Los Chacayes 2019

dos.name: San Pablo
rules: 100% of the grapes from the delimited zone, from varieties suited to quality wine (Law 25.163). Recognized by RESOL-2019-10-APN-INV#MAGYP.
Lies within the Uco Valley GI; its western boundary is the 1,700 m contour line.
dos.soil: Alluvial fan of the Las Tunas River: medium-sized stones and gravel with abundant calcareous material and a build-up of calcium carbonate.
dos.climate: Cool mountain zone beside the Cordillera Frontal, between about 1,150 and 1,700 m, with low average temperatures and a wide diurnal range.
dos.txt: One of the coolest terroirs in the Uco Valley: it excels in taut whites (Chardonnay) and Malbec with black fruit and silky tannins.
dos.sources: INV, listado de IG y DOC de la República Argentina (18/04/2024) (RESOL-2019-10-APN-INV#MAGYP); Zuccardi, Guía del terroir del Valle de Uco y ficha Fósil 2021; La Nación, Tres regiones ganan fuerza; El Cuco Digital, IG Tunuyán y Tupungato

dos.name: Vista Flores
rules: 100% of the grapes from the delimited zone, from varieties suited to quality wine (Law 25.163). Recognized by INV Res. C.11/2012.
Lies within the Uco Valley GI.
dos.soil: Mainly sandy-loam soils with plenty of rounded stones, sometimes calcareous.
dos.climate: High-altitude desert; the highest vineyards, to the west, reach about 1,200 m.
dos.txt: Produces the fleshiest, ripest Malbecs in the Uco Valley, with plum, violet and rose.
dos.sources: INV, listado de IG y DOC de la República Argentina (18/04/2024) (Res. INV C.11/2012); Decanter, Malbec Mendoza sub-zones

dos.name: Agrelo
rules: 100% of the grapes from the delimited zone, from varieties suited to quality wine (Law 25.163). Recognized by INV Res. C.21/2005.
Lies within the Luján de Cuyo department (and GI).
dos.soil: Sandy, stony soils of Andean origin.
dos.climate: Desert, with barely about 200 mm of rain a year; vineyards between about 780 and 1,100 m.
dos.txt: Approachable, deeply colored Malbec with black fruit (fig) and soft, sweet tannins.
dos.sources: INV, listado de IG y DOC de la República Argentina (18/04/2024) (Res. INV C.21/2005); Decanter, Malbec Mendoza sub-zones

dos.name: Las Compuertas
rules: 100% of the grapes from the delimited zone, from varieties suited to quality wine (Law 25.163). Recognized by INV Res. C.30/2007.
Lies within the Luján de Cuyo department (and GI), in the west, bordering Vistalba and Perdriel.
dos.soil: Alluvial, with sand and stones carried by the river from the Andes; some sectors have clay, silt and rounded stones.
dos.climate: Warm desert moderated by altitude (about 1,100 m) and cool mountain breezes.
dos.txt: An area of century-old Malbec vineyards: broad, ripe wines with firm acidity and the structure to age.
dos.sources: INV, listado de IG y DOC de la República Argentina (18/04/2024) (Res. INV C.30/2007); Decanter, Malbec Mendoza sub-zones; iProfesional, Durigutti en Las Compuertas

dos.name: Pedernal Valley
rules: 100% of the grapes from the delimited zone, from varieties suited to quality wine (Law 25.163). Recognized by INV Res. C.21/2007.
dos.soil: Calcareous clays of marine origin with limestone, dolomite and black flint; on the Tontal slope, flint stones.
dos.climate: Pre-Andean (Precordillera) valley at about 1,200–1,550 m, moderately cool (about 1,600 degree-days), with a diurnal range of about 15 °C.
dos.txt: Malbec with an austere, calcareous profile, high-altitude Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, and herbal Sauvignon Blanc.
dos.sources: INV, listado de IG y DOC de la República Argentina (18/04/2024) (Res. INV C.21/2007); Wines of Argentina, San Juan: from bulk production to premium labels; Wines of Argentina, The Pedernal Valley, San Juan's open secret; Diario de Cuyo, Los vinos de altura del Valle de Calingasta

dos.name: Calingasta Valley
rules: 100% of the grapes from the delimited zone, from varieties suited to quality wine (Law 25.163). Calingasta GI by INV Res. C.32/2002; Valle de Calingasta recognized as a synonym by INV Res. C.41/2013.
Within the valley are the Barreal GI (INV Res. C.42/2013) and the Hilario, Sorocayense and Tamberías GIs (2023).
dos.soil: Stony, clay-poor soils typical of an arid climate.
dos.climate: High valley between the Andes and the Precordillera, at about 1,350–1,700 m, with about 80 mm of rain (in summer) and a diurnal range of up to 24 °C.
dos.txt: Fresh mountain reds and whites from criolla grapes from century-old vineyards, especially in Barreal.
dos.sources: INV, listado de IG y DOC de la República Argentina (18/04/2024) (Res. INV C.32/2002, C.41/2013, C.42/2013, RESOL-2023-35/36/37-APN-INV#MEC); Bichos de Campo, Tres IG en Calingasta; Wines of Argentina, San Juan: from bulk production to premium labels; Diario de Cuyo, Los vinos de altura del Valle de Calingasta

dos.name: Zonda Valley
rules: 100% of the grapes from the delimited zone, from varieties suited to quality wine (Law 25.163). Recognized by INV Res. C.04/2015 (Official Gazette, 20/04/2015), delimited by four geographic points.
Valley about 18 km west of the city of San Juan, between the San Juan River and the Cuesta de los Colorados.
dos.soil: Loam soils; in the upper La Ciénaga sector, calcareous soils.
dos.climate: Wide diurnal range; in La Ciénaga, at about 1,700 m, the cool southerly wind lowers the average temperature.
dos.txt: Syrah with notes of leather, smoke and earth, spicy Malbec and well-adapted Petit Verdot.
dos.sources: INV, listado de IG y DOC de la República Argentina (18/04/2024) (Res. INV C.04/2015, argentina.gob.ar/normativa); Diario de Cuyo, Las uvas y vinos del Valle de Zonda logran reconocimiento; Diario de Cuyo, El enoturismo ayuda difundir varietales del Valle de Zonda; Wines of Argentina, San Juan: from bulk production to premium labels

dos.name: Famatina Valleys
dos.area: La Rioja: valleys between the Velasco and Famatina ranges (Chilecito and surroundings)
rules: 100% of the grapes from the delimited zone, from varieties suited to quality wine (Law 25.163). Recognized by INV Res. C.29/2004.
Valleys that take in several La Rioja localities and form a single wine-growing area; they hold most of La Rioja's vineyards.
dos.climate: Hot semi-arid oasis, with mild nights, little rain and severe drought; the Chilecito valley lies at about 900 m.
dos.txt: Highly aromatic Torrontés Riojano (orange blossom, rose, citrus) and deeply colored reds from Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Bonarda and Syrah.
dos.sources: INV, listado de IG y DOC de la República Argentina (18/04/2024) (Res. INV C.29/2004); Wines of Argentina, La Rioja (ficha provincial) y The wines of La Rioja

dos.name: Calchaquí Valleys
dos.area: Salta, Tucumán and Catamarca: a system of intermontane valleys about 270 km long
rules: 100% of the grapes from the delimited zone, from varieties suited to quality wine (Law 25.163). Recognized by INV Res. C.37/2002; Valle Calchaquí recognized as a synonym by INV Res. C.16/2010.
Interprovincial zone that contains, among others, the Cafayate Valley GI (60% of its planted area).
dos.soil: Mostly sandy-loam or sandy, with many stones in the subsoil and very good drainage.
dos.climate: Vineyards between about 1,530 and 3,111 m (Payogasta), dry, very sunny days and cold nights with a very wide diurnal range.
dos.txt: High-altitude Malbec and Torrontés, now fresher and more precise, plus Criollas from old pergola vineyards and high-altitude Sauvignon Blanc.
dos.sources: INV, listado de IG y DOC de la República Argentina (18/04/2024) (Res. INV C.37/2002 y C.16/2010); Wines of Argentina, Salta (ficha provincial), Rediscovering the Calchaquí Valleys y The Calchaquí Valleys

dos.name: Humahuaca Gorge
rules: 100% of the grapes from the delimited zone, from varieties suited to quality wine (Law 25.163). Recognized by INV Res. C.39/2015.
dos.soil: Highly varied depending on the slope and mountain of each vineyard, in plots of a few hectares.
dos.climate: High-altitude desert on the Tropic of Capricorn, about 60 ha between 2,200 and 3,330 m, with less than 150 mm of rain and a 20 °C diurnal range; frost risk.
dos.txt: Concentrated yet fresh reds from Malbec, Syrah and Tannat, and herbal, pungent Sauvignon Blanc.
dos.sources: INV, listado de IG y DOC de la República Argentina (18/04/2024) (Res. INV C.39/2015); Wines of Argentina, Quebrada de Humahuaca wines y Jujuy (ficha provincial)

dos.name: Upper Río Negro Valley
dos.area: Río Negro: Río Negro valley (General Roca, Fernández Oro, Mainqué, Valle Azul)
rules: 100% of the grapes from the delimited zone, from varieties suited to quality wine (Law 25.163). Recognized by INV Res. C.37/2002.
Holds about 60% of Río Negro's vineyards.
dos.soil: Alluvial, poor and well drained, with stone, sand, clay and calcium carbonate, between the river and the bardas (plateau escarpments).
dos.climate: Continental and dry, at about 370 m and latitude 38–39° S, with little rain, wind and a wide diurnal range.
dos.txt: Reds with a good alcohol-acidity balance and old-vine Malbec; fine Pinot Noir in Mainqué and historic Semillón.
dos.sources: INV, listado de IG y DOC de la República Argentina (18/04/2024) (Res. INV C.37/2002); Wines of Argentina, Río Negro (ficha provincial), Wines of Río Negro y Mainqué Patagonian Pinot Noir

dos.name: Chapadmalal
dos.area: Buenos Aires: General Pueyrredón district (Atlantic coast)
rules: 100% of the grapes from the delimited zone, from varieties suited to quality wine (Law 25.163). Recognized by INV Res. C.20/2014.
dos.soil: Low hills and rolling ridges; the vineyards are planted on the hilltops, where leaching by rain leaves poorer soils.
dos.climate: Oceanic, humid, windy and with a low diurnal range; about 3 km from the sea and 35 m above sea level, with enough rain for dry farming.
dos.txt: Fresh, aromatic whites (Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Albariño), Pinot Noir and sparkling wines; it is the country's easternmost GI.
dos.sources: INV, listado de IG y DOC de la República Argentina (18/04/2024) (Res. INV C.20/2014); Wines of Argentina, Buenos Aires (ficha provincial), Wines of Buenos Aires y Vineyards of Buenos Aires; SommTV, Atlantic coast of Argentina

dos.name: Pampa El Cepillo
dos.area: Mendoza: San Carlos department (Uco Valley), south of Paraje Altamira
rules: Wines from varieties recognized by the INV as suited to quality wine (INV Res. C.32/2002, art. 4). Recognized by RESOL-2019-1-APN-INV#MAGYP (Official Gazette, 17/09/2019).

Bounded to the north by the Paraje Altamira GI, to the east by National Route 40, to the south by the historic boundary of the Estancia El Cepillo and to the west by Calle Constantini, where the Cordón El Cepillo GI begins (RESOL-2022-7-APN-INV#MEC).
dos.soil: Sandy-loam soils with a high calcium carbonate content.
dos.climate: An extreme zone for cold, above 1,000 m: it usually records the lowest minimum temperatures in the Uco Valley, with a wide diurnal range and irrigation with snowmelt water.
dos.txt: Aromatically intense reds, with black and red fruit and floral touches, high freshness and firm tannins, from one of the coldest corners of the Uco Valley.
dos.sources: INV, listado de IG y DOC de la República Argentina (18/04/2024); RESOL-2019-1-APN-INV#MAGYP y RESOL-2022-7-APN-INV#MEC (argentina.gob.ar/normativa); El Cuco Digital, IG parte I: So Bustos; Marcasur, Pampa El Cepillo recognized as a GI

dos.name: Tulum Valley
dos.area: San Juan: Tulum Valley, in the south of the province
rules: Wines from varieties recognized by the INV as suited to quality wine, with a yield of no less than 130 kg of grapes per 100 l (INV Res. C.32/2002, art. 4). Recognized ex officio by INV Res. C.32/2002.
The resolution only names the area; it sets no boundaries.
dos.soil: Alluvial, sandy and clay soils, permeable; a 1976 survey identified nine soil types of viticultural interest.
dos.climate: Dry and temperate, at about 600 m; vineyards require irrigation.
dos.txt: San Juan's main wine valley: it produces everything from table wines to fine and fortified wines; Syrah is the best-adapted noble grape, with aromatic concentration and a fleshy body.
dos.sources: INV, listado de IG y DOC de la República Argentina (18/04/2024); Res. INV C.32/2002 y C.23/1999 (argentina.gob.ar/normativa); Welcome Argentina, Vinos de San Juan; Grassin et al., Viticultural zoning San Juan (IVES)

dos.name: Barreal
rules: Wines from varieties recognized by the INV as suited to quality wine (INV Res. C.32/2002, art. 4). Recognized by INV Res. C.42/2013 (Official Gazette, 20/05/2014), delimited by coordinates.
Lies within the Calingasta Valley GI; in 2014 it had 13 ha of vines in three vineyards.
dos.climate: High-altitude valley: the Entre Tapias winery sits at 1,650 m, in a valley with vineyards between 1,400 and 1,700 m and a short frost-free period.
dos.txt: Young wines with deep colors and vibrant aromas, with balanced acidity; also whites and rosés from Criolla Chica and Moscatel from old vineyards.
dos.sources: INV, listado de IG y DOC de la República Argentina (18/04/2024); Res. INV C.42/2013 (argentina.gob.ar/normativa); Diario de Cuyo, Barreal ya cuenta con identificación geográfica; Diario de Cuyo, Los vinos de altura, emblema del Valle de Calingasta

dos.name: Alto Agrelo
dos.area: Mendoza: Luján de Cuyo department, along Route 40 south of its junction with Route 7
rules: Grapes and winemaking from the polygon delimited by the INV. Recognized by RESOL-2025-27-APN-INV#MEC (Official Gazette, 23/07/2025), at the request of Grupo Avinea.
The fifth GI in Luján de Cuyo, alongside Agrelo, Las Compuertas, Luján de Cuyo and Vistalba.
dos.climate: High-altitude desert: it reaches about 1,150 m and is the highest GI in Luján de Cuyo; the east–west slope increases sun exposure.
dos.txt: Very dark grapes with more tannin: concentrated Malbec and Cabernet Franc, from the highest sector of Agrelo.
dos.sources: RESOL-2025-27-APN-INV#MEC (argentina.gob.ar/normativa) y su polígono oficial (Google My Maps); Marval, Nueva indicación geográfica para vinos; Bichos de Campo, El INV reconoció Alto Agrelo; The Drinks Business, Alto Agrelo awarded GI status

dos.name: Temperate Valleys
dos.area: Jujuy: temperate valleys centered on Perico (El Carmen, Pampa Blanca and the capital)
rules: Grapes and winemaking from the polygon delimited by the INV. Recognized by RESOL-2025-28-APN-INV#MEC (Official Gazette, 02/09/2025), at the request of the government of Jujuy.
According to the INV, 13 producers and 15.3 ha of vines; El Carmen has the largest area.
dos.climate: More humid and warmer than the Humahuaca Gorge, with a diurnal range of up to about 12 °C, cloud cover during ripening and rain at harvest; among the earliest harvests in the country.
dos.txt: Fruity, fresh, light wines with marked natural acidity: good whites, sparkling bases and young reds with less color than those of the Quebrada.
dos.sources: RESOL-2025-28-APN-INV#MEC (argentina.gob.ar/normativa) y su polígono oficial (Google My Maps); Mendoza Post, Valles Templados: la nueva IG que reconoció el INV; Bichos de Campo, Volveré a Jujuy: Valles Templados

dos.name: Cordón El Cepillo
dos.area: Mendoza: San Carlos department (Uco Valley), south of Paraje Altamira and west of Pampa El Cepillo, up to the 1,400 m above sea level contour
rules: Recognized by RESOL-2022-7-APN-INV#MEC (Official Gazette, 26/12/2022), at the request of Bodegas Esmeralda S.A.; the INV dismissed the opposition filed by Grupo Peñaflor S.A.

Bounded to the north by the Paraje Altamira GI, to the east by Calle Constantini (where the Pampa El Cepillo GI begins), to the south by the historic boundary of the Estancia El Cepillo and to the west by the 1,400 m contour; the resolution sets 28 vertices.
dos.txt: The highest, westernmost strip of El Cepillo, resting against the piedmont up to 1,400 metres: the INV separated it from Pampa El Cepillo as a terroir in its own right, suited to quality wines.
dos.sources: INV, listado de IG y DOC de la República Argentina (18/04/2024); RESOL-2022-7-APN-INV#MEC (argentina.gob.ar/normativa, norma 377091)
